paper.title: When inequality means equity: horizontal wage dispersion and the propensity to leave current employment across different organizational settings
paper.code_data_availability: No data or code availability statement and no Statistics Denmark project number are printed. …

registers.name_in_paper: Danish Integrated Database for Labor Market Research (IDA, maintained by Statistics Denmark)
registers.role: sample frame, linkage, treatment and outcome variables, controls
cross-check of the classification of individuals into hierarchical levels
industry dummies (controls) and the industry exclusion rule

registers.name_in_paper: date at which the legal identity of the firm disappeared (firm closure)
registers.role: robustness check: Cox model of firm exit and removal of employees of exiting firms

linkages: individuals linked to employers and establishments through the IDA matched employer-employee structure, annually
a mobility event is recorded only when BOTH the firm identifier and the establishment identifier change, so that mergers and acquisitions do not generate spurious transitions

employees classified into up to four firm hierarchical levels (top management, middle management, mid-level skilled, low-level unskilled) using Statistics Denmark's occupational groups, cross-checked with DISCO codes

sample.universe: employees in the Danish labour market: 1,637,012 employees in 84,118 firms identified in 2003 and traceable between 1998 and 2002
sample.unit_of_observation: individual-year (firm-individual-year) observations in an unbalanced discrete-time duration panel
selection_rules: only employees who were newly hired in 2002, to avoid left-censoring and equalize tenure

removed employees working in industries that tended to be highly regulated or where wage practices were less likely to be a choice of the firm (agriculture, electricity, water collection, public sector, schools, hospitals, waste, associations)
excluded employees younger than 24 years or older than 60 in 2002
removed employees working for firms with less than seven employees
excluded firms with only one hierarchical level in 2003
removed firms for which wage dispersions could not be calculated for one or more years due to missing wage values
sample.period: 2003-2008 (window of investigation); employment history from 1998; wage regression 2002-2008
sample.n_individuals: 132,778 newly hired individuals in 2002 employed by 9140 firms

construction_notes: Horizontal wage dispersion: Gini coefficient computed for each hierarchical level with the standard formula printed as Equation (1) (p. 125): G = (2 * sum_{i=1}^{n} i * wage_i) / (n * sum_{i=1}^{n} wage_i) - (n + 1)/n; firm-level dispersion is the average of the Gini coefficients across all hierarchical layers; the Gini ranges from 0 (absolute equality) to 1 (absolute inequality).

Mincer wage regression on log wages with education, age and age squared, female dummy, Danish-citizen dummy, tenure with the current firm, hierarchical levels, reference year and firm fixed effects, estimated on all individuals working in the private sector 2002-2008 (12,274,499 individual-year observations); the covariates explained approximately 38% of the total observed variation in wages (Supplementary Table A3).
AWD = Gini of the PREDICTED values of the Mincer regression; UWD = Gini of the RESIDUALS of the Mincer regression.
Employment tenure treated as categorical, 1 to 5, with 5 covering employees with 5 or more years of tenure.
Wage-dispersion variables are included using lagged values; the authors report that non-lagged values would have little to no effect.
Firm size = logarithm of the number of employees. Decentralization = share of employees in the lower levels of the hierarchy relative to the top level.
Wage earnings expressed in 2002 Danish Kroner; work experience (years worked 1998-2002) entered at standardized values with a squared term.
Large firms = more than 500 employees; small firms = less than 100 employees (alternative thresholds of 50 and 25 tested).
Of the 132,778 newly hired employees, 105,923 (79.8%) left their 2002 workplace within the 2003-2008 window.
No control for individual age is included because of collinearity with wage experience.

claims.statement: Unattributable horizontal wage dispersion is negatively associated with the hazard of an employee leaving the employer they joined in 2002 (main-effects model, no interactions).

register_source.value: IDA (Danish Integrated Database for Labor Market Research, Statistics Denmark)

definition.value: Gini coefficient (Equation 1, p. 125) of wages within each of the firm's hierarchical levels, averaged across the firm's hierarchical layers, computed on the RESIDUALS of a Mincer log-wage regression (education, age, age squared, female, Danish citizenship, tenure category, hierarchical level, year, firm fixed effects); captures pay variation not explained by observable characteristics. Entered with lagged values.

timing.value: firm-level, lagged value relative to the individual-year observation, 2003-2008

register_source.value: IDA (Danish Integrated Database for Labor Market Research, Statistics Denmark)

definition.value: binary indicator of a first-time job transition away from the employer the employee joined in 2002; a mobility event is defined when both the firm and the establishment identifier changed, so that mergers and acquisitions are not counted. In the discrete-time duration model the baseline outcome is remaining with the 2002 employer.

timing.value: annual, individual-year observations 2003-2008 (discrete-time hazard, unbalanced panel)

units.value: change in the log-odds (logit coefficient) of leaving the 2002 employer in a given year, per one-unit change in the regressor (the wage-dispersion Ginis run on a 0-1 scale)

estimand.target_population: Employees newly hired in 2002 at Danish private-sector firms with at least seven employees and more than one hierarchical level in 2003, aged 24-60 in 2002, outside highly regulated industries, tracked annually 2003-2008 until they left the employer they joined in 2002
estimand.time_horizon: annual hazard of leaving the 2002 employer over the 6-year window 2003-2008

population.description: Employees newly hired in 2002 at Danish private-sector firms with at least seven employees and more than one hierarchical level in 2003, aged 24-60 in 2002, outside highly regulated industries, tracked annually 2003-2008 until they left the employer they joined in 2002
population.selection: conditioned on being newly hired in 2002 (to avoid left-censoring) and on the firm surviving the wage-dispersion construction; employees of firms with fewer than seven employees, of firms with a single hierarchical level, and of highly regulated industries (agriculture, electricity, water collection, public sector, schools, hospitals, waste, associations) are excluded

identification.source_of_variation: Cross-firm and cross-individual variation in horizontal wage dispersion (Gini of Mincer-residual and of predicted wages within hierarchical levels), firm size and decentralization among Danish private-sector employees newly hired in 2002. No experiment, lottery or discontinuity is used; the authors state they could not exploit a natural experiment providing exogenous variation.

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional on the included firm-level and individual-level controls, the industry dummies and (outside Table 5) the year dummies, the explanatory variable is independent of unobserved determinants of the employee's outcome -- i.e. the regression adjusts for all relevant confounders.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Not asserted positively. The authors instead concede they cannot rule out omitted variables (p. 140) and offer a one-to-one nearest-neighbour matching exercise at firm and individual level whose results are unaltered (p. 137).

key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated at p. 135; supported by re-running the analysis excluding 2003 (probation-period dismissals) and by removing employees of firms that subsequently exited (Supplementary Tables A8, A9), with results virtually unaltered.

key_assumptions.assumption: Coworkers at the same hierarchical level in the same firm are the employee's relevant social comparison reference group, and the Gini of Mincer residuals (UWD) captures pay variation that rewards unobserved differences in individual contributions.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Argued from equity / social comparison theory (Section 2.2) and from the residual approach used in past studies of wage dispersion (p. 126); individual productivity is never observed.

key_assumptions.assumption: Large and small firms are comparable in terms of their wage dispersions (common support across the firm-size split).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated at p. 137 together with the acknowledgement that descriptive statistics show significant differences in UWD and AWD between small and large firms; addressed with 366-to-366 firm-level and 2087-employee individual-level nearest-neighbour matching.

key_assumptions.assumption: Absent the 2006 wage-transparency law, the change in employees' hazard of leaving would not have differed systematically across levels of unattributable wage dispersion, firm size and decentralization (common-trend restriction on counterfactual means).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Never stated or tested. The authors instead argue that time dummies capture changes in baseline hazard rates and that attrition differences across levels of wage dispersion are unlikely (p. 140).

key_assumptions.assumption: The 2006 law was unanticipated, so that behaviour before 2006 does not respond to it.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated at p. 132: 'The adoption of the law was essentially unforeseen, constituting a shock.'

implies_edges.from: Danish wage-transparency law (June 2006)

key_assumptions.assumption: Exposure to the shock within the duration sample is not distorted by before-shock attrition (the employees still at risk after 2006 are not a selected group in a way that varies with wage dispersion).
key_assumptions.supported_by: Raised by the authors as a limitation (p. 140): 'non-random exposure to the exogenous shock among subjects since the remaining subjects hardly can be considered random'; they argue any resulting bias is negligible.
